answers.answer:
In SCOPe 2.08 the histone-fold relatives are all in a single superfamily, so the relationship is superfamily-level homology. Class a (all-alpha) > Fold a.22 "Histone-fold" (sunid 47112) > Superfamily a.22.1 "Histone-fold" (sunid 47113). a.22 contains only this one superfamily. Nucleosome core histones are only one of five families in a.22.1:

- a.22.1.1 Nucleosome core histones (sunid 47114): H2A, H2B, H3, H4 and macro-H2A.1 histone domain, plus automated matches. These are the eukaryotic histones themselves.
- a.22.1.2 Archaeal histone (sunid 47129). The protein is 'Archaeal histone' (sunid 68897), for example Methanothermus fervidus histones A and B. These are the prokaryotic-type homologs of eukaryotic core histones and are distant relatives. In most archaea they form histone-fold dimers that wrap DNA in a nucleosome-like way.
- a.22.1.3 TBP-associated factors, TAFs (sunid 47134). These are histone-fold domains in transcription and chromatin factors, not DNA-packaging histones. The proteins include TAF(II)42, TAF(II)62, TAF(II)28, TAF(II)18, TAF(II)-135/hTAF4 and TAF(II)-20/hTAF12, negative cofactor 2 (NC2) alpha and beta, NF-Y subunits B and C (Nf-Yb3, Nf-Yc2), Chrac-14 and Chrac-16, and the histone domain of Son of sevenless (SOS). Histone-fold proteins pair through the handshake motif into heterodimers, as H3-H4 and H2A-H2B do.
- a.22.1.4 Bacterial histone-fold protein (sunid 101318). These are hypothetical proteins such as Aq_328 (Aquifex) and TTHA1479 (Thermus). They show that the fold also occurs in bacteria, but their function is not established by classification alone.
- a.22.1.0 automated matches (sunid 238448), which are machine-assigned entries.

Evolutionary strength: the different families inside a.22.1 are placed together by structural and functional evidence of probable common ancestry despite low sequence identity. This is superfamily-level homology. Only members of the same family, such as H3 with H3 or H2A with H2B, have clear sequence-level relationships. The fold level (a.22) adds nothing beyond the superfamily here, because there is only one superfamily, so the fold and superfamily statements coincide. The class level (all-alpha) is only a coarse structural grouping and is not evidence of relatedness.

Limits: sharing the histone fold does not mean shared function. TAFs, NC2, NF-Y, CHRAC and SOS domains do not necessarily form nucleosomes or package DNA like core histones. Do not transfer functional, binding or templating conclusions between families without direct evidence, and do not infer the roles of the bacterial hypothetical proteins from the fold alone.

Not in the relationship: many proteins named 'histone' or acting on histones are unrelated by fold. Examples are the histone H1/H5 linker globular domain and Hho1p (a.4.5.13, winged-helix fold in a different class-a fold), histone deacetylase HDAC8 (c.42.1.2) and histone methyltransferase Dot1l (c.66.1.31). Their names or substrates mention histones, but they are not homologs of the histone fold.

In SCOPe 2.08 the histone-fold relatives are all in a single superfamily, so the relationship is superfamily-level homology. Class a (all-alpha) > Fold a.22 "Histone-fold" (sunid 47112) > Superfamily a.22.1 "Histone-fold" (sunid 47113). a.22 contains only this one superfamily. Nucleosome core histones are only one of five families in a.22.1:

- a.22.1.1 Nucleosome core histones (sunid 47114): H2A, H2B, H3, H4 and macro-H2A.1 histone domain, plus automated matches. These are the eukaryotic histones themselves.
- a.22.1.2 Archaeal histone (sunid 47129). The protein is 'Archaeal histone' (sunid 68897), for example Methanothermus fervidus histones A and B. These are the prokaryotic-type homologs of eukaryotic core histones and are distant relatives. In most archaea they form histone-fold dimers that wrap DNA in a nucleosome-like way.
- a.22.1.3 TBP-associated factors, TAFs (sunid 47134). These are histone-fold domains in transcription and chromatin factors, not DNA-packaging histones. The proteins include TAF(II)42, TAF(II)62, TAF(II)28, TAF(II)18, TAF(II)-135/hTAF4 and TAF(II)-20/hTAF12, negative cofactor 2 (NC2) alpha and beta, NF-Y subunits B and C (Nf-Yb3, Nf-Yc2), Chrac-14 and Chrac-16, and the histone domain of Son of sevenless (SOS). Histone-fold proteins pair through the handshake motif into heterodimers, as H3-H4 and H2A-H2B do.
- a.22.1.4 Bacterial histone-fold protein (sunid 101318). These are hypothetical proteins such as Aq_328 (Aquifex) and TTHA1479 (Thermus). They show that the fold also occurs in bacteria, but their function is not established by classification alone.
- a.22.1.0 automated matches (sunid 238448), which are machine-assigned entries.

Evolutionary strength: the different families inside a.22.1 are placed together by structural and functional evidence of probable common ancestry despite low sequence identity. This is superfamily-level homology. Only members of the same family, such as H3 with H3 or H2A with H2B, have clear sequence-level relationships. The fold level (a.22) adds nothing beyond the superfamily here, because there is only one superfamily, so the fold and superfamily statements coincide. The class level (all-alpha) is only a coarse structural grouping and is not evidence of relatedness.

Limits: sharing the histone fold does not mean shared function. TAFs, NC2, NF-Y, CHRAC and SOS domains do not necessarily form nucleosomes or package DNA like core histones. Do not transfer functional, binding or templating conclusions between families without direct evidence, and do not infer the roles of the bacterial hypothetical proteins from the fold alone.

Not in the relationship: many proteins named 'histone' or acting on histones are unrelated by fold. Examples are the histone H1/H5 linker globular domain and Hho1p (a.4.5.13, winged-helix fold in a different class-a fold), histone deacetylase HDAC8 (c.42.1.2) and histone methyltransferase Dot1l (c.66.1.31). Their names or substrates mention histones, but they are not homologs of the histone fold.
